rationale: A broad scouting gradient should reveal the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. Starting at 40 C leaves room to adjust temperature in either direction for selectivity.

Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shortening the gradient by one step tests whether we can retain full resolution while reducing run time, with the original method as the benchmark.

The shorter gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves the critical pair close to the resolution threshold. Raising temperature at fixed gradient tests whether temperature selectivity can improve that pair and shorten elution further.
At 50 C all pairs remain fully resolved, so test the next shorter gradient to seek a faster method with the same maximum CRF. Comparing against injection 3 isolates the effect of gradient steepness.

Narrowing the solvent window restores nearly the gradient slope of the fully resolved 8-minute method while retaining a 6-minute gradient. The slightly higher starting organic fraction should reduce early waiting time, and the final fraction remains above the observed elution window.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving its slope to reduce retention time without substantially compressing the critical pair. Injection 5 provides a fully resolved benchmark for checking whether the higher starting organic fraction compromises early separation.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention while using a slightly shallower slope to protect the critical pair. The final fraction remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction of 0.51, allowing a shorter programmed gradient.

Reduce the gradient slope one grid step to lift the marginal R = 1.46 pair above 1.5 while preserving early-pair selectivity. The last peak should remain inside the gradient, with retention still shorter than the fastest fully resolved method so far.

Shift the fully resolved injection 8 window upward by 0.05 while keeping its slope fixed to shorten elution. This tests whether its resolution margin can accommodate a higher starting organic fraction without losing early-pair or critical-pair separation.

Make the gradient one step shallower than injection 9 to restore critical-pair resolution while retaining its shorter initial retention. This should preserve early-pair separation and may yield a faster fully resolved method than injection 8.

Maximum CRF is already secured, so test a distinctly faster selectivity regime rather than only refining the current boundary. A steep gradient and lower temperature may carry the critical pair through an elution-order reversal and restore separation, while low starting organic protects early retention.

Test a higher starting organic fraction in the fast-gradient regime to shift the central pair away from co-elution. Raising temperature relative to injection 11 may also separate its late pair while keeping the last peak near two minutes.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction and modestly lower temperature improve the central pair in the fast-gradient regime. The lower temperature should help preserve early retention, while injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Test the upper temperature limit with a moderate gradient slope to seek a faster fully resolved selectivity regime. The lower starting organic fraction protects early retention while we check whether temperature-induced reordering separates or merges the early peaks.

Explore a lower-temperature, higher-starting-organic window to test whether altered selectivity can resolve the central pair in a short run. The shallower slope than injection 13 should spread the late peaks, while the lower temperature helps retain the early compounds.

Shift injection 15's window upward at unchanged slope to test whether the central pair separates further in the reversed-order regime. Early retention is already weak, so this is a boundary test; injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Keep injection 16's starting composition and temperature but halve the gradient slope to measure the central pair's response in this selectivity regime. The lower endpoint should still elute all compounds promptly, while avoiding further compression of the early pair from a higher starting organic fraction.

Return to the fully resolved selectivity regime of injection 10, using a slightly shallower two-minute gradient followed by a hold. This should protect the central pair while testing whether a lower-endpoint hold can preserve maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Compare directly with injection 10 to measure temperature selectivity near the fastest fully resolved method. Lowering temperature should improve early-pair separation; the central pair's response will show whether this provides room for further gradient compression.

Use the improved early-pair separation at 45 C to permit a higher starting organic fraction, while making the slope shallower to protect the central pair. This tests a narrower elution window for full resolution near the current fastest maximum-CRF method.

Refine around injection 10 with a slightly shallower slope, seeking more critical-pair resolution margin while keeping the last peak near 3.5 minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured, so this tests a nearby, potentially more robust fully resolved method.

Test a slope between injections 7 and 8 to locate the full-resolution boundary more precisely. The slightly shallower gradient than injection 7 should lift its R = 1.46 central pair above threshold while eluting the last peak sooner than injection 8.

Test a more balanced resolution margin by lowering injection 8's temperature one step. The early pair should gain separation, while the central pair's existing margin may preserve maximum CRF with all peaks still eluting well before 10 minutes.

Reduce injection 10's endpoint one step to increase its narrow central-pair resolution margin while preserving early selectivity. This should retain maximum CRF and provide a more forgiving alternative to the fastest fully resolved method.

Lower injection 24's temperature one step to improve its limiting early-pair separation, using the central pair's resolution margin to accommodate the selectivity shift. This final refinement targets a well-resolved maximum-CRF alternative; injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.
